note: 35 practitioner interviews and 435 tools reviewed, the best available map of where audit tooling actually falls short.
title: Towards AI Accountability Infrastructure: Gaps and Opportunities in AI Audit Tooling
journal: Proceedings of the CHI Conference on Human Factors in Computing Systems
explain_beginner: Companies and outside researchers who want to check whether an AI system is safe or fair rely on software tools built for that purpose, everything from bias measurement libraries to documentation generators. This study asks whether those tools actually help someone hold an AI system accountable, not just measure it. The researchers interviewed 35 people who do this kind of AI auditing for a living and separately reviewed 435 existing tools built for AI evaluation and oversight. They found that most tools are good at one thing, measuring a system against a standard, but weak at the parts of accountability that come before and after measurement, actually discovering that a system is causing harm in the first place, and using evidence of harm to push for something to change. The interviews also surfaced a second, more mundane problem, practitioners said the tools that do exist are often genuinely hard to use in a real audit. The study does not test whether building better tools for those missing steps would actually work, it only shows that almost nothing currently exists to try.
explain_business: Organizations building an internal AI audit function should not assume that adopting evaluation software, bias metrics, model documentation generators, monitoring dashboards, is the same as building accountability, this research finds those categories are the best served part of the market while the tools needed to actually surface a harm once it happens or push a fix through an organization barely exist yet. In practice this means a compliance team should budget separately for the human process of harms discovery and remediation tracking rather than expecting a purchased tool to cover it, since the study finds the tooling market has not caught up to that need. It also means teams should expect friction and staff training overhead even from the evaluation tools they do buy, since practitioners in the study reported real usability problems with existing options, not just coverage gaps. This applies now to any team standing up an AI audit program, and the actionable takeaway is to treat tool purchases as covering evaluation only, with harms discovery and follow through built as an internal process until better tooling exists.
explain_practitioner: This paper combines 35 semi structured interviews with AI audit practitioners and a landscape review of 435 tools used across the AI audit ecosystem to compare what practitioners actually need against what tooling currently exists. The central finding is a gap between two clusters, tools that support evaluation and standard setting are relatively mature, while tooling for harms discovery, the work of actually finding that a system is causing damage, and advocacy, using evidence to compel a fix, is sparse to nonexistent. The interviews separately document concrete usability friction practitioners hit even with the evaluation tools that do exist, not just coverage gaps. Unlike a benchmark study, this paper reports no accuracy or performance number, its contribution is the mapping itself, and a real limitation is that the 35 interview subjects and 435 catalogued tools represent a snapshot of practitioners and tools the authors could reach, not a verified census of the field, so the size of the harms discovery and advocacy gap is a directional finding rather than a precisely measured one.
